title: Future Reference and Sequence of Tenses
orientation: Future meaning is expressed through several grammatical resources, not one interchangeable formula. A timetable, an appointment, a promise and a prediction may concern the same date while presenting different kinds of information. In this lesson you will connect those purposes with will, shall, be going to and present forms used for future reference. You will then build combinations that place an activity within a future interval or look back from a future boundary. The final module connects these choices to reporting and subordinate clauses, where a change of viewpoint matters more than a demand to keep every verb identical. Read the foundational patterns first and compare the interpretations beside each example. In the activities, specify what is known, intended or merely predicted, and avoid changing the strength of a commitment while editing its form.
outcomes: Choose and explain future expressions for plans, offers, schedules and predictions.
Form negatives and questions with will and be going to.
Build future progressive, perfect and perfect-progressive sequences.
Distinguish a time adjunct clause from an embedded question.
Report a future-from-past viewpoint while preserving dates and communicative force.

modules.title: Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment
modules.definition: English uses several constructions to refer to future time. Will and shall are modal auxiliaries, while be going to combines a form of be with going to and a plain-form verb. Their meanings overlap but their use depends on the speaker’s purpose and viewpoint.
foundation: Use will with the base form: The driver will return. Add not for a negative, The driver will not return, and put will before the subject for a question, Will the driver return? The contraction will not becomes won’t. A promise, prediction, offer and decision can all use will: I will return your call; The river will rise; I will carry that bag; I will take the early train. The word future identifies the intended time, not a guarantee that a prediction is factually certain. Identify what the speaker is doing as well as when the event is expected.
intermediate: Be going to commonly highlights an intention already held or evidence visible now: We are going to replace the roof; Those loose tiles are going to fall. Its finite be agrees with the subject: I am, she is, they are. Make negatives and questions with be: They are not going to move; Are they going to move? Going to need not describe physical travel. Compare They are going to the clinic, where to the clinic is a destination phrase, with They are going to inspect the clinic, where inspect belongs to the intended action. Keep these different structures separate.
advanced: Will and going to often both fit the same future event, with a different conversational emphasis. I will call her can make a decision or commitment; I am going to call her can state a prior intention. A context may favour one without making the other structurally impossible. Shall with I and we remains possible for formal future reference, especially in British English, though will is more widespread. Shall I open the window? offers action or asks what the speaker should do; Shall we begin? proposes joint action. These questions have a modal purpose, not merely an announcement of future time.
expert: Future expressions interact with modality: they present expectations, intentions and commitments from the speaker’s current standpoint. A spontaneous decision is a useful context for teaching will, not a test proving that will can never describe an earlier plan. Likewise, visible evidence favours going to without banning will from evidence-based predictions. Informal gonna represents a reduced pronunciation of going to in the intended-action construction; it is unsuitable as a default spelling in formal reports. A careful transformation preserves the communicative force: changing I promise I will help into I may help weakens commitment, even though both clauses are grammatically formed.

patterns.meaning: Modal future reference; interpretation may include prediction, willingness, decision or commitment.
Common intention or evidence-based prediction construction.

examples.sentence: I will send the receipt tonight.
examples.analysis: Will can express the speaker’s commitment to a future action.

examples.sentence: The panels are going to fall if the supports move again.
examples.analysis: The prediction is presented in relation to an existing dangerous condition.

examples.sentence: Shall we discuss the draft before lunch?
examples.analysis: This is a proposal about joint action, an established British use of shall.

contrasts.b: I am going to ask the curator.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first may announce a decision or promise; the second commonly foregrounds an intention already held.

exceptions: The form going to can describe destination rather than intention: We are going to Lahore contains a destination phrase. Do not analyse every occurrence as a future auxiliary construction.

mistakes.problem: She will to send the figures.
mistakes.reason: Core modal will selects a base form without infinitival to.

mistakes.problem: They is going to review the application.
mistakes.repair: They are going to review the application.
mistakes.reason: Finite be agrees with plural they; going to does not replace agreement.

glossary.definition: Interpretation concerning a time later than the relevant viewpoint.
glossary.example: The ferry leaves tomorrow uses a present form for future reference.

glossary.definition: The degree to which a speaker undertakes or supports a proposition or action.
glossary.example: I promise I will help makes a commitment.

modules.title: Present forms for arrangements, timetables and future facts
modules.definition: Present-tense forms can have future reference. Present progressive commonly presents an arrangement, while present simple commonly presents a timetable, fixed schedule or future fact. These uses rely on context and do not create new verb endings.
foundation: Consider The interview starts at nine tomorrow. Starts is present tense, but tomorrow places the event in the future. A timetable, programme or scheduled event commonly uses present simple: The coach departs at six; The term ends in July. Negative and question formation stays the same as for present simple: The coach does not stop here; When does the coach leave? Be also keeps its ordinary present forms: The ceremony is on Friday. A future time expression helps the reader recognise the intended reference; without one, the surrounding conversation may supply it.
intermediate: Present progressive commonly presents an arrangement: I am meeting the surveyor at ten; We are moving next month. An arrangement can involve other people, a booking, or the speaker’s own settled plan; another person need not appear in every sentence. Build it with finite be and an -ing form, and form questions and negatives with be. Compare Are you meeting the surveyor? and You are not meeting the surveyor today. The construction presents the action as planned or arranged from the present viewpoint. It does not assert that the future is immune to cancellation or disruption.
advanced: A single event can be described as schedule or arrangement: The delegation leaves on Thursday and The delegation is leaving on Thursday may both be natural. The first can report its programme, while the second draws attention to an arrangement in progress. An objective item should not ask for the only correct form when both readings are available. Present progressive is not the ordinary neutral choice for a bare speculative prediction such as a distant weather guess; will or going to normally serves that purpose. Context may support marked conversational uses, so explain the default rather than invent an absolute prohibition.
expert: Form and temporal interpretation are distinct levels of analysis. A present-tense schedule can concern one future occasion, not an eternal habit: The eclipse begins at 14:10 tomorrow. Present simple also occurs in subordinate time clauses such as when the train arrives, a structure studied in the final module of this day. Do not confuse that syntactic pattern with a main-clause timetable merely because both verbs look present. When editing, preserve the source of certainty: The timetable says the train leaves at six explicitly attributes the schedule; I expect the train will leave at six expresses an expectation. Both are grammatical but make different claims.

patterns.meaning: Commonly presents a schedule, fixed programme or future fact.
Commonly presents a current arrangement for a later event.

examples.sentence: The examination begins at nine on Monday.
examples.analysis: Present begins reports an official schedule with future reference.

examples.sentence: We are interviewing two applicants tomorrow.
examples.analysis: The progressive presents an arrangement already established.

examples.sentence: The timetable says the last bus departs at 22:15, but we are leaving earlier.
examples.analysis: A stated schedule and a personal arrangement coexist without requiring identical constructions.

contrasts.a: The team flies to Muscat on Tuesday.
contrasts.b: The team is flying to Muscat on Tuesday.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical in suitable contexts: programme or schedule versus current arrangement.

exceptions: Present simple can refer to a unique future fact, not only a repeated timetable: Her birthday falls on a Sunday next year. Do not require repetition where the context supplies a fixed future occurrence.

mistakes.problem: What time the train does leave tomorrow?
mistakes.repair: What time does the train leave tomorrow?
mistakes.reason: A direct present-simple question places does before the subject.

mistakes.problem: We are meet the architect tomorrow.
mistakes.repair: We are meeting the architect tomorrow.
mistakes.reason: A progressive arrangement requires the -ing form after are.

glossary.definition: A plan presented as settled or organised in the relevant context.
glossary.example: I am seeing the dentist tomorrow presents an appointment.

glossary.definition: A use of present simple to report a scheduled event.

modules.title: Future progressive, perfect and perfect progressive
modules.definition: Future-oriented auxiliary combinations can present an activity in progress at a later point, a situation viewed from that later point, or the duration of earlier activity up to it. The construction and the temporal context must both be considered.
foundation: Future progressive uses will be plus an -ing form: At ten tomorrow, I will be interviewing applicants. It places the reader within an activity expected to be in progress at that point. Negate the finite modal, I will not be interviewing, and invert it in a question, Will you be interviewing? Do not change be to is after will: a modal selects the base form. This construction can also present an expected course of events, as in I will be passing the pharmacy, so I can collect the prescription. The intended time is supplied by the context.
intermediate: Future perfect uses will have plus a past participle: By ten, I will have interviewed three applicants. It looks back from a future boundary and presents what will then be completed or true. A state can also extend to that boundary: By June, she will have known him for ten years. Future perfect progressive uses will have been plus -ing: By ten, I will have been interviewing for two hours. It draws attention to activity and its duration up to the future viewpoint. It does not necessarily state that the activity stops at that boundary.
advanced: Compare completed quantity with continuing course: By Friday, we will have inspected six bridges reports a completed total; By Friday, we will have been inspecting bridges for a week highlights the period of activity. Neither construction alone guarantees the whole project is finished unless the project’s limits are stated. With some predicates, both future perfect simple and progressive are defensible: In May, I will have worked here for five years and I will have been working here for five years can describe the same employment period. A question must specify the desired construction or intended focus if it is to have a unique answer.
expert: The so-called future perfect is a combination of modal will and perfect have; its conventional label describes a common temporal interpretation. A deadline does not automatically make it obligatory: We will finish by Friday is ordinary English beside We will have finished by Friday. The latter explicitly adopts a later retrospective viewpoint. Progressive restrictions also remain sensitive to meaning: will have known is the ordinary form for a continuing knowledge state, while will have been considering describes a process. Avoid mechanically generating all possible auxiliaries for every verb. A formally elaborate sequence can be semantically awkward even when the component endings appear in the correct order.

patterns.meaning: An activity viewed as in progress at a future point.
A retrospective view from a future point.
Activity and its duration leading up to a future viewpoint.

examples.sentence: At this time tomorrow, the committee will be hearing evidence.
examples.analysis: The future point lies within the projected hearing activity.

examples.sentence: By the end of tomorrow, the committee will have heard six witnesses.
examples.analysis: The future perfect presents a completed count by the boundary.

examples.sentence: By noon, the volunteers will have been working for four hours.
examples.analysis: The perfect progressive foregrounds duration without necessarily ending the work at noon.

contrasts.a: We will finish the audit by Friday.
contrasts.b: We will have finished the audit by Friday.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical promises or predictions in context. The second explicitly views completion retrospectively from the future boundary.

exceptions: Some duration predicates allow either simple or progressive perfect forms with overlapping reference: will have lived and will have been living can both measure a period up to a future point. A duration phrase does not alone select one uniquely.

mistakes.problem: At eleven, they will are discussing the report.
mistakes.repair: At eleven, they will be discussing the report.
mistakes.reason: After will, use base be, not are.

mistakes.problem: By July, she will have wrote three chapters.
mistakes.repair: By July, she will have written three chapters.
mistakes.reason: Perfect have selects the past participle written, not past-tense wrote.

glossary.definition: A conventional label for will/shall have plus past participle with a common later-retrospective interpretation.
glossary.example: By dusk, we will have arrived.

glossary.definition: A will/shall be + -ing construction commonly used for activity at a future point.
glossary.example: At dusk, we will be travelling.

modules.title: Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints
modules.definition: Future reference is relative to a viewpoint. A past narrator can describe an event that was still future then. Time and condition clauses follow their own patterns, and reporting may shift a viewpoint without requiring every verb to become the same tense.
foundation: Future in the past describes a later situation viewed from an earlier past point: On Monday, she said she would return on Tuesday. Would is the usual backshifted counterpart of will in this reporting pattern. Past forms of other future expressions are also available: She was going to return; She was leaving the next day. The construction does not by itself establish that the planned return happened. Add the outcome if it matters: She was going to return, but the storm cancelled the ferry. Identify the earlier viewpoint before deciding what a later expression means.
intermediate: In ordinary future time clauses, use a present form rather than future will: I will call when the meeting ends; We will leave after she has signed the register. Present perfect in the time clause can emphasise prior completion. The main clause can still contain will. Similar teaching patterns occur with open conditions: If the weather improves, we will leave. This guidance concerns a particular subordinate use; it is not a ban on will after the spelling when or if. Distinguish a clause locating an event from an embedded question asking what time an event will occur.
advanced: Compare I will phone when the train arrives with I do not know when the train will arrive. The first when-clause supplies the time of phoning; the second is an embedded interrogative complement expressing an unknown arrival time. Will is appropriate in that embedded question. In an if-clause, will may express willingness or insistence rather than simple future location: If you will hold the ladder, I can carry the tools. This means if you are willing to hold it. A later lesson develops the full range of conditional meanings. Do not remove a modal mechanically when it carries such an independent meaning.
expert: Backshift is common after past reporting verbs, but reporting also considers whether a statement remains true or a plan remains future at report time. She said the office opens at nine can retain a currently valid schedule; She said the office opened at nine adopts a past reporting viewpoint without necessarily asserting that the schedule changed. Choose and explain the viewpoint. Temporal consistency is coherence, not uniform tense: Yesterday I learned that the exhibition opens next month contains a past discovery and a future schedule. Time and place words also depend on the reporting context. Use explicit dates when a transformation would otherwise make tomorrow, next week or the following day ambiguous.

patterns.form: past reporting verb + would + base form
main future clause + when/after/until + present form
patterns.meaning: Common future time-clause pattern; not the pattern of every clause introduced by the same word.

examples.sentence: The witness said she would send the photographs the next day.
examples.analysis: Would presents sending as future from the earlier statement.

examples.sentence: We will publish the report after the auditors have checked the figures.
examples.analysis: The present perfect time clause presents checking as prior to publication.

examples.sentence: I cannot tell you when the report will appear.
examples.analysis: The when-clause is an embedded question, so future will is appropriate.

contrasts.a: I will wait when she arrives.
contrasts.b: I wonder when she will arrive.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first clause locates waiting; the second expresses an unknown arrival time.

exceptions: Will can occur in a conditional clause with willingness: If you will sign here, we can proceed. Explain its modal meaning instead of teaching never use will after if.

mistakes.problem: I will contact you when the ordinary scheduled meeting will end.
mistakes.repair: I will contact you when the ordinary scheduled meeting ends.
mistakes.reason: For this intended future time-clause reading, present ends is the neutral pattern.

mistakes.problem: She said she would to bring the original documents.
mistakes.repair: She said she would bring the original documents.
mistakes.reason: Modal would takes the base form without to.

glossary.definition: A change to a past-oriented form when reporting from a past viewpoint.
glossary.example: Will return can be reported as would return.

glossary.definition: A later situation presented from an earlier past viewpoint.
glossary.example: She knew she would leave the next morning.

questions.prompt: Which is a correctly formed will-construction?
options: She will to inspect the roof.
questions.why: Will takes the base form inspect without to or an -s/past ending.

questions.prompt: In Shall we begin?, what is a common British English function of shall?
questions.why: Shall we commonly makes a proposal about joint action; the sentence is not a perfect or past report.

questions.prompt: Which analysis of We are going to review the lease is accurate?
options: The construction can present a prior intention.
Are is an infinitive after a modal.
To review is a destination phrase.
questions.why: Be going to plus a base verb can foreground a prior intention; no physical travel is required.

questions.prompt: The timetable says The ferry departs at 07:20 tomorrow. Which judgement is accurate?
options: The sentence states a repeated event only.
A present-simple schedule can refer to a future event.
Departs must be replaced by will depart.
A present form cannot have future reference.
questions.why: Present simple is established for timetables and future fixed occurrences. No mechanical replacement is required.

questions.prompt: Complete the explicitly requested present-progressive arrangement: We ____ the architect tomorrow.
questions.why: Are meeting is finite be plus -ing, used here for an arrangement; the other sequences are malformed.

questions.prompt: Which construction is future perfect progressive?
questions.why: Will have been waiting combines will, perfect have, participial been and progressive waiting.

questions.prompt: Use a future-perfect construction: By Friday, the editor will have ____ all six chapters.
questions.why: Read is the past participle as well as the base spelling of this irregular verb. Have requires the participle here.

questions.prompt: Check the intended willingness reading: If you will hold the ladder, I can carry the tools. Which judgement is accurate?
options: No error: will can express willingness in the condition.
Remove will because it is impossible after if.
Replace hold with held while keeping the intended willingness meaning unchanged.
questions.why: Will is not merely a future-time marker here; it means are willing to. The proposed absolute prohibition is false.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an embedded question about a future arrival time?
options: I will stand up when the guest arrives.
When the guest arrives, we will begin.
We will wait until the guest arrives.
I wonder when the guest will arrive.
questions.why: Wonder selects an embedded interrogative expressing an unknown time; the other subordinate clauses locate main-clause events.

questions.prompt: Form the requested normal backshifted report: On Monday she said she ____ on Tuesday. Use would plus leave.
questions.why: Would selects base leave. The task requests a backshifted pattern rather than claiming backshift is obligatory in every reporting context.

questions.prompt: Identify a likely communicative function of I will carry that box for you, said when someone is struggling with it.
questions.model: It is an offer of help, made through a will-construction.
rubric: Relate the function to the stated situation.
Do not label every will-clause a neutral prediction.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Complete with forms of be in the going-to construction: I ____ going to apply; she ____ going to apply; they ____ going to apply.
questions.model: I am going to apply; she is going to apply; they are going to apply.
rubric: Use am/is/are according to the subjects.
Keep apply in its base form.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain a possible difference in emphasis between I will ask him and I am going to ask him. State why both may be grammatical.
questions.model: The first can announce a decision or commitment; the second commonly foregrounds an intention already held. Context may support both rather than identifying one as structurally wrong.
rubric: Give a meaning or discourse contrast.
Acknowledge overlap and avoid an absolute rule about when decisions were made.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Distinguish going to in We are going to the archive and We are going to inspect the archive.
questions.model: In the first, to the archive gives a destination for going. In the second, going to plus inspect presents an intended future action.
rubric: Identify the noun-phrase destination versus the base verb.
Do not assign the future-intention pattern solely from the words going to.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Arrange a direct timetable question: does / leave / the last train / when ?
questions.model: When does the last train leave?
rubric: Place does before the subject.
Use base leave after does.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Give suitable contexts for The delegation leaves on Tuesday and The delegation is leaving on Tuesday.
questions.model: The first can report the official programme; the second can present its current travel arrangement. Both can describe the same future trip.
rubric: Supply schedule versus arrangement viewpoints.
Do not invent a different departure day or claim that one form guarantees the event.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Write a sentence using present simple for a unique future fact rather than a repeated habit.
questions.model: The anniversary falls on a Thursday next year.
rubric: Use an actual present-simple form.
Make the future reference and unique occurrence clear.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Build all three forms of inspect: At ten tomorrow they will ____ ____; by noon they will ____ ____ three sites; by noon they will ____ ____ ____ for four hours.
questions.model: At ten tomorrow they will be inspecting; by noon they will have inspected three sites; by noon they will have been inspecting for four hours.
rubric: Use be inspecting, have inspected and have been inspecting.
Distinguish in-progress viewpoint, completed count and duration.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Compare At six, she will be writing the report and By six, she will have written the report.
questions.model: The first puts six within projected writing activity; the second presents completion no later than six from a future viewpoint.
rubric: Relate at to the in-progress viewpoint and by to completion.
Do not infer that the first also guarantees a finished report.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain why By next June, I will have known her for twenty years normally uses known rather than been knowing.
questions.model: Know in its ordinary acquaintance or knowledge sense is stative. The future perfect simple can measure a continuing state up to a future viewpoint.
rubric: Identify the stative interpretation.
Recognise that a long duration does not force a progressive.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Can We will finish by Friday be grammatical without the future perfect? Explain the viewpoint difference from We will have finished by Friday.
questions.model: Yes. The simple will-construction can give a deadline. The future perfect more explicitly looks back from the future boundary to completion.
rubric: Accept the non-perfect construction.
Explain retrospective viewpoint rather than making by an automatic tense signal.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the when-clauses in I will call when the train arrives and I do not know when the train will arrive.
questions.model: The first is a time adjunct clause locating the call; the second is an embedded interrogative complement expressing an unknown arrival time.
rubric: Identify time adjunct versus embedded question.
Explain why future will in the second is appropriate.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Use a present-perfect time clause: We will release the payment after the engineer ____ ____ the work. Use approve.
questions.model: We will release the payment after the engineer has approved the work.
rubric: Use has approved in the time clause.
Present approval as prior to payment release.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: What does She was going to attend, but the ferry was cancelled establish about intention and outcome?
questions.model: It establishes a past intention to attend and a later ferry cancellation. The construction was going to alone would not prove attendance; the context points to disruption without explicitly reporting every subsequent action.
rubric: Separate the past intention from actual fulfilment.
Do not infer an unstated replacement journey or attendance.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Edit only faulty verb sequences: She said she would to return on Friday. The ferry leaves at nine tomorrow. We will wait until the office opens.
questions.model: She said she would return on Friday. The ferry leaves at nine tomorrow. We will wait until the office opens.
rubric: Remove to after modal would.
Retain the legitimate timetable and present-form future time clause.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: A colleague says on Monday The office opens at nine. You report this on Tuesday as She said the office opens at nine. Is the retained present automatically an error?
questions.model: No. The reporter can present the schedule as still valid. Opened would be a common backshifted alternative without necessarily implying a changed schedule.
rubric: Recognise context-dependent retention of present tense.
Do not assert that backshift always signals falsity or change.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Write an offer with will and a proposal with Shall we. Explain the communicative purpose of each.
questions.model: I will take your coat. This offers help. Shall we review the agenda first? This proposes joint action.
rubric: Use will plus base form for the offer.
Use Shall we plus base form for the proposal.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim: Every sentence containing for ten years must use future perfect progressive when it refers to next year. Give a counterexample.
questions.model: The claim is false. By next year, she will have owned the house for ten years uses future perfect simple with a possession state.
rubric: Produce a grammatical future-perfect simple state example.
Explain that duration and aspect are distinct.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: He will to explain the procedure.
rubric: Remove infinitival to after will.
Preserve the future action and subject.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: We is going to replace the damaged chair.
corrections.model: We are going to replace the damaged chair.
rubric: Make finite be agree with we.
Keep replace as the base form.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: The managers are meet the auditor on Tuesday.
corrections.model: The managers are meeting the auditor on Tuesday.
rubric: Use the -ing form in the intended progressive arrangement.
Keep the stated Tuesday appointment.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: At noon tomorrow, I will am interviewing the witnesses.
corrections.model: At noon tomorrow, I will be interviewing the witnesses.
rubric: Use base be after will.
Retain the in-progress future viewpoint.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: By May, the team will have complete the survey.
corrections.model: By May, the team will have completed the survey.
rubric: Use the past participle completed after perfect have.
Preserve the future retrospective boundary.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct the intended ordinary future time clause: I will write to you after the hearing will end.
corrections.model: I will write to you after the hearing ends.
rubric: Use a present form in the stated time-clause reading.
Do not remove will from the main clause.
alternatives: I will write to you after the hearing has ended.

corrections.prompt: Decide whether correction is required: I do not know when the shipment will arrive.
corrections.model: No change is required. When the shipment will arrive is an embedded question about a future time.
rubric: Identify the embedded interrogative complement.
Do not apply the ordinary future time-adjunct pattern to every when-clause.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Decide whether correction is required: According to the published timetable, the lecture begins tomorrow at ten.
corrections.model: No change is required. Present simple can report a scheduled future event.
rubric: Retain the source-attributed schedule.
Do not demand will solely because tomorrow occurs.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

transformations.prompt: On Monday, Rina said I will return on Tuesday. Report her statement on Wednesday, retaining the explicit days and normal backshift.
transformations.model: On Monday, Rina said that she would return on Tuesday.
rubric: Use would plus base return for the requested backshift.
Preserve Monday as reporting event and Tuesday as intended return date.
alternatives: On Monday, Rina said she would return on Tuesday.

transformations.prompt: Express the same completion promise with an explicit future-retrospective viewpoint: We will finish the inspection by Friday.
transformations.model: We will have finished the inspection by Friday.
rubric: Use will have plus past participle finished.
Retain the deadline and completion promise.
alternatives: By Friday, we will have finished the inspection.

writing.prompt: Write a 90–130-word plan for a public event. Include an attributed schedule, a personal arrangement, a commitment, activity in progress at a future point, and completion viewed from a future deadline. Include one time clause.
writing.model: The programme says the exhibition opens at ten on Saturday. I am meeting the volunteers at eight to check the signs and the entrance. I will bring the spare name badges, as promised. At nine, the technicians will be testing the microphones while the volunteers arrange the chairs. By the time the doors open, we will have checked every public entrance. We will admit visitors after the safety officer has approved the route. If a display needs repair, the organisers will close that area rather than promise access before it is safe. The plan allows time for a final review.
rubric: Separate a source-attributed timetable from a personal arrangement.
Use will to express a commitment without changing it into a possibility.
Build future progressive and perfect forms correctly.
Use an appropriate present form in the future time clause.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 5: In The visitors will have arrived, identify the modal, perfect auxiliary and lexical participle.
recall.model: Will is the finite modal; have is the perfect auxiliary in its base form; arrived is the lexical past participle.
rubric: Distinguish auxiliary functions.
Do not label arrived as an independent finite verb here.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 8: What difference does by rather than until normally create in Finish the work by Friday versus Continue working until Friday?
recall.model: By sets a deadline for completion; until gives an endpoint for continuation.
rubric: Distinguish completion deadline and duration endpoint.
Preserve the separate predicates rather than mechanically swapping prepositions.
